Pip, whose full name is Phillip Pirrip, is the protagonist of Charles Dickens's Great Expectations. He is an orphan boy whose desire to escape his humble origins and win the love of an unattainable girl drives him toward self-destruction. His journey from innocence through illusion to hard-won moral reckoning makes him one of literature's great coming-of-age figures, embodying the tension between ambition and authenticity.

An orphan raised by his sister and her blacksmith husband Joe in the Kent marshes, Pip works as an apprentice despite yearning for something grander. He falls in love with Estella, the beautiful, icy ward of the wealthy Miss Havisham, and becomes convinced this is his great expectation—his destined path to gentility. He receives an anonymous fortune, which he assumes comes from Miss Havisham, and he abandons Joe to become a London gentleman, ashamed of his humble past.

He discovers too late that his benefactor is actually Magwitch, an escaped convict he once helped as a child. This discovery destroys his illusions about the source and meaning of his expectations. His shame at Magwitch's identity and his obsessive devotion to Estella lead him toward ruin—emotionally, financially, and morally. Eventually he reconciles with Joe and learns to value integrity over social aspiration. His growth involves accepting, not escaping, his past.

Pip's moral education unfolds throughout the novel in Great Expectations itself. Miss Havisham, the wealthy eccentric whose house and affection he mistakes for the source of his great expectations, represents false promise. Estella, the beautiful woman he loves but who is emotionally incapable of returning his affection, becomes the object of a pursuit that mirrors his pursuit of false expectations. Charles Dickens uses him to explore social ambition and the costs of shame. His coming of age exemplifies the literary mode of moral development through disillusionment. Magwitch, the convict whose rescue by Pip as a child echoes throughout the story, is revealed as his true benefactor.
